rq: Is air connectivity clean connectivity? Trade and openness have ambiguous effects on the environment because scale, composition and technique effects pull in different directions (Grossman and Krueger 1993; Antweiler, Copeland and Taylor 2001; Managi, Hibiki and Tsurumi 2009). This paper asks a narrower question: when a country becomes more central in the global air network, does the pollution and carbon intensity of its economy fall, and if so through which of the three channels?

Air connectivity is measured with the Global Air Connectivity Index (GACI), a within-year standardised composite of degree, betweenness, closeness, eigenvector and regional-importance centrality of each airport, aggregated to the country by seat-weighted mean. Because aviation itself emits under 3% of national CO2 and a negligible share of SO2, any effect on national intensities must run through the economy, not through aircraft.

Hypotheses. H1 (clean connectivity): higher air connectivity lowers SO2, NOx and CO2 per unit of GDP and raises the renewable share. H2 (technique, not composition): the reduction occurs within fuels, as lower emissions per unit of fuel burned, and is not explained by shifts in industrial structure. H3 (where): the effect is concentrated in goods-producing economies that have plants and power stations to retrofit, not in service economies.

Design. Country-year panel, 176 countries, 1996–2023 (unified sample: ln GACI, controls, SO2, NOx, CO2 and energy intensities and the instrument observed; SO2 and NOx from CEDS v_2025_03_18). ln y = b ln GACI + ln pop + ln GDP pc + (ln GDP pc)^2 + country FE + year FE, standard errors clustered by country. All denominators come from one source (WDI GDP in constant 2015 US$ = GDP per capita × population; OWID/EI energy; CEDS v2025 SO2 and NOx; OWID CO2), so the log identities ln X/GDP = ln X/pop − ln GDP/pop and ln SO2/GDP = ln E/GDP + ln CO2/E + ln SO2/CO2 hold exactly and the coefficients add up across tables. Panel A of each table is fixed-effects OLS; Panel B is 2SLS with GACI instrumented by Feyrer-type air market access, which interacts a country's fixed geography (great-circle distances to all other markets relative to sea distances) with world-wide air-traffic growth, so that it moves only with global technology and not with the country's own policies or outcomes. The GACI coefficient is an elasticity; one within-country standard deviation of ln GACI is 0.07, so a one-SD move changes an outcome by about 7% of the coefficient.
T1: Air connectivity is associated with cleaner production per unit of GDP for local pollutants: a 1% higher GACI lowers SO2 intensity by 0.7% and NOx intensity by 0.3%, and raises the renewable share of final energy by 8 points per log unit (the electricity share moves in the same direction but is imprecise). The CO2 and energy-intensity coefficients are negative but not significant, and the fuel mix does not move. One within-country SD of connectivity translates into 5% lower SO2 intensity. Because ln GDP per capita is a control, the per-GDP and per-capita columns have identical GACI coefficients, as they must. Panel B (air market access, first-stage F 11.7) confirms every sign; SO2, NOx and renewables stay significant and CO2 intensity is significant at 10%. Extending the sample from 2019 to 2023 with the 2025 CEDS release lowers the SO2 coefficient from −0.86 to −0.71 (Appendix Table 1a), because the effect is concentrated before 2010.
T2: Table 2 isolates the technique term of Table 1b by fuel. Coal use does not fall (col 1), yet SO2 per unit of oil consumed falls by 1.0% per 1% of GACI (col 3, Energy Institute fuel data, 77 countries) and SO2 per unit of coal- and oil-CO2 falls by 0.8–0.9% (cols 4–6, all countries). Because these emission factors depend only on the sulphur content of the fuel and on end-of-pipe desulphurisation, the same inputs are being used more cleanly. In the 2023 sample process SO2 (smelting, refining) also falls at the 10% level (−0.54), so it is a weaker placebo than in the 2019 sample, where it was zero; we note this rather than hide it. Panel B confirms the oil emission factor (−6.9, F 11.8); in the fuel-consumption subsamples the instrument has no power (F below 2.5) and those IV estimates are uninformative.
T3: Adding industrial composition, openness and urbanisation moves the GACI coefficient by about 10%: in the OLS panel composition itself explains essentially nothing (−1% to +8%), openness 2–13% and urbanisation 2–7%. Panel B repeats the decomposition for the 2SLS coefficient with the auxiliary regressions also estimated by 2SLS, so the identity holds exactly; the explained shares are small and of mixed sign, and the full IV coefficient is larger than the base one. The composition channel emphasised in the pollution-haven literature is not what drives the result; with Tables 1b and 2 this leaves technique as the operative channel.
T4: In the 1996–2023 sample the goods-economy interaction remains large and significant for renewables (+15 points) and CO2 intensity (−0.42) but is no longer significant for SO2 and NOx (−0.73 and −0.25, SE 0.47 and 0.18), although the signs are unchanged. The income-tercile split is uninformative. Panel B splits the IV by economy type; point estimates have the same ordering as OLS but the subsample first stages are weak (F 3–4), so the split-sample IV is suggestive only. The heterogeneity evidence is therefore weaker than in the 2019 sample and should be presented as such.
T5: This table takes the IV magnitude seriously, as a referee will. The reduced form (outcome on the instrument directly) is negative and significant for SO2, NOx and CO2 and positive for renewables, so the IV sign does not depend on the first-stage scaling. The measurement-error IV instruments the seat-weighted ln GACI with the unweighted country mean of airport GACI (F 18), a classical correction that needs no exclusion restriction beyond independent measurement error: it roughly doubles the OLS coefficient (SO2 −1.4), which says that about a third of the gap between OLS (−0.7) and the market-access IV (−4.9) is attenuation. The remaining gap is either a local average effect for geography-driven connectivity gains or a violation of the exclusion restriction; Appendix Table 3 shows the market-access instrument draws its power from Europe.
A1a: The SO2 result survives Managi-style controls (capital-labour ratio) and a geographic sea-connectivity control, is unchanged when 2020–2021 are excluded (−0.71), and is strongest in 1996–2009 (−0.82**). It is zero in 2010–2023 (+0.03) and under every region-by-year specification (GACI macro-regions, UN continents, UN subregions, region trends, income-tercile-by-year). The 1996–2019 estimate on the same CEDS 2025 data is −0.86**, and −1.02*** with the CEDS 2022 release, so about a third of the earlier coefficient was data vintage and the rest is the post-2010 period. GACI is a relative, within-year index, so region-by-year designs remove much of its variation; together with the absence of an effect after 2010, this is the main open issue of the paper.
A1b: The CO2-intensity coefficient is negative but not significant in the base specification and in every alternative, and changes sign under region-by-year effects. CO2 is the expected weak outcome of the mechanism: desulphurisation does not reduce CO2, and Table 1b shows the only CO2 channel is energy efficiency.
A2: Results are not an artefact of the aggregation rule. The seat-weighted mean of airport GACI and its level give the same picture; the unweighted mean across all airports is smaller and weaker, because it dilutes hub airports with many small ones.
why: Openness reaches a country through two physical networks that carry different things. Ships move goods: over 80% of world trade by volume travels by sea, and the goods that travel by sea are the heavy, energy- and pollution-intensive ones (ores, fuels, steel, chemicals, cement). Aircraft move people and ideas: almost all intercontinental passenger travel is by air, and air cargo is about a third of world trade by value but under one percent by weight (IATA), concentrated in electronics, pharmaceuticals and precision machinery. The trade-and-environment literature measures openness with trade volumes, which bundle these two networks together and therefore cannot tell whether the environmental effect of openness comes from the goods that arrive by ship or from the people and knowledge that arrive by plane.

Air connectivity isolates the people-and-knowledge channel. Business travel is a documented engine of technology diffusion (Hovhannisyan and Keller 2015), new direct air links raise firm-to-firm connections and local growth (Campante and Yanagizawa-Drott 2018), face-to-face contact is necessary for trading complex goods and services (Cristea 2011), and the opening of airspace increased trade in exactly the goods that need in-person coordination (Söderlund 2023). Abatement technology is this kind of knowledge: flue-gas desulphurisation, low-sulphur refining, combined-cycle plants and wind and solar projects are installed by vendors, engineers, consultants and financiers who travel, and the standards that mandate them are copied by regulators who meet. If air connectivity transmits anything to the environment, the technique effect is where it should appear.

The question matters for policy because aviation is regulated for its own emissions. Ticket taxes, ETS coverage and route restrictions are justified by aircraft CO2, which is about 2.5% of the global total. Our companion paper on European aviation taxes finds that these taxes reduce seats and connectivity at small airports. Whether that is a net environmental gain depends on whether connectivity has an economy-wide clean effect that the aircraft-only accounting omits. For developing countries the same question arises in reverse: open-skies agreements and airport investment are evaluated on tourism and trade, and an environmental co-benefit through faster adoption of clean technology would change that evaluation.

GACI is the right measure for this question because it captures a country's position in the network, not the volume of its traffic. It is a within-year standardised composite of degree, betweenness, closeness, eigenvector and regional-importance centrality of each airport, so a country's value rises when its airports become better connected to the rest of the network relative to other countries' airports. That is the relevant object for knowledge flows: what matters is who a country's firms, engineers and officials can reach in a day, not how many seats depart. Seat volume (Appendix Table 2) and the geographic sea-connectivity controls (Appendix Table 1) are reported to show that the results come from network position rather than from traffic or from maritime access.
gaci_title: What GACI is and how to read it

gaci.text: GACI (Global Air Connectivity Index) is an airport-level index of position in the world air network, built from OAG scheduled-service data for about 3,500 airports a year, 1996–2024. For each year the scheduled network is a weighted graph: nodes are airports, edges are routes, edge weights are seat capacity. Five centrality measures are computed for every airport: degree (number of destinations), flow betweenness (how much indirect traffic routes through the airport, the hub measure), closeness (how few connections are needed to reach the rest of the network), eigenvector centrality (connection to other well-connected airports) and regional importance (the airport's share of its region's capacity). Figure 1(a) illustrates the objects on a toy network; a hub such as HKG scores high on betweenness because flows between Europe and Australasia pass through it.

The five measures are combined by principal components within each year. Figure 1(b) shows that the first component carries 73–77% of the variance and loads almost equally on the five measures (weights 0.38–0.49) in every year, so GACI is in effect an equally weighted standardised average of the five centralities. Because the PCA is run year by year on standardised inputs, GACI is a relative measure: it tells us where an airport stands in that year's network, not how many flights it has. An airport whose traffic grows at the world average rate keeps a constant GACI; GACI rises only when the airport becomes more central relative to others.
gaci.cap: Figure 1. Construction of GACI. (a) Network objects on a toy graph. (b) Year-by-year first-principal-component loadings and variance share, 1996–2023.

gaci.text: For the country-level analysis we take the seat-weighted mean of GACI across a country's airports (cwm) and use its log. Weighting by seats means the index describes the airports that actually carry the country's traffic; Appendix Table 2 shows that the unweighted mean, which gives a small regional field the same weight as the main hub, is a weaker regressor. Figure 2 shows the country series for six economies. Germany and the United States are flat, because their position was already central and grew with the world. The UAE, Türkiye, China and Ethiopia rise steeply as Dubai, Istanbul, the Chinese secondary cities and Addis Ababa became hubs. This is the within-country variation the fixed-effects regressions use: a country's GACI changes when its network position changes relative to the rest of the world.
gaci.cap: Figure 2. ln GACI (seat-weighted country mean) for six countries, 1996–2023.

gaci.text: Two consequences for reading the tables. First, the within-country standard deviation of ln GACI is small, 0.07, because most countries' relative position moves slowly; coefficients therefore look large per log unit and should be read as effects of a 7% change in connectivity, which is roughly what Türkiye or China achieved in a typical five-year window. Second, because GACI is relative and within-year standardised, designs that compare countries only within their own region-year or income-group-year remove much of its variation (Appendix Table 1); we report them as the boundary of the country panel.

Figure 3 shows the main result as a binned scatter. Both axes are residuals after country and year fixed effects and the income and population controls (Frisch–Waugh–Lovell), so each point is the mean of about 180 country-years with similar connectivity residuals. The downward slope in panel (a) is the Table 1 coefficient on SO2 intensity; panel (b) shows the same relation for SO2 per unit of CO2, the sulphur-intensity-of-carbon term that carries three quarters of the effect in Table 1b. The relation is approximately linear and is not driven by a few extreme bins.
gaci.cap: Figure 3. Binned scatter of the within-country relation between ln GACI and (a) ln SO2/GDP, (b) ln SO2/CO2. Unified sample, 176 countries, 25 bins; line is the regression slope.

gaci.text: Figure 4 maps the tables onto the scale–composition–technique decomposition that organises the paper. Scale and composition are tested and rejected in Tables 2 and 3; technique is where the effect appears. Table 4 says where (goods-producing economies), Table 5 confirms the direction with an instrument.
gaci.cap: Figure 4. Which table tests which channel.

agg_title: Global aggregate: what the elasticity implies

agg.text: Figure 5 puts the two sides of the result on a map. Panel (a) is the change in ln GACI between the first and last year a country appears in the unified sample (1996 to 2023 for most). Connectivity gains were largest in the Gulf, Türkiye, China, Korea and Eastern Europe, and were negative in parts of Latin America, the Sahel and conflict countries (Syria, Yemen, Venezuela). Panel (b) is the observed change in ln SO2/GDP over the same window. The two maps are mirror images in East Asia, the Gulf and Europe, where connectivity rose and SO2 intensity collapsed; they also agree in the countries where connectivity fell and SO2 intensity did not improve.
agg.cap: Figure 5. (a) Change in ln GACI and (b) observed change in ln SO2/GDP, first to last sample year. Grey: outside the unified sample.

agg.text: A back-of-the-envelope aggregate follows from the Table 1 elasticity. Holding each country's connectivity at its initial level and applying the point estimate of −0.71 to its observed change in ln GACI, SO2 emissions in 2023 would have been about 11 Mt higher than observed, which is 17% of final-year SO2 in the sample and roughly a quarter of the 39 Mt decline recorded between 1996 and 2023. The 95% band runs from 1 Mt (3% of the decline) to 23 Mt. In tonnes the implied reduction is dominated by China, India, Russia, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye.

This exercise is an accounting illustration, not a causal decomposition of the global SO2 decline: it extrapolates a within-country elasticity linearly to changes two to three times the within-country standard deviation, and it attributes to connectivity whatever the fixed-effects regression attributes to it. Its purpose is to show that the coefficient is economically meaningful at the scale of the actual network changes of the period, not that air connectivity explains half of global desulphurisation.

T1b: This table makes the accounting explicit. Column 1 is decomposed exactly into energy intensity (col 2), carbon intensity of energy (col 3) and sulphur intensity of carbon (col 4): −0.71 = −0.15 − 0.02 − 0.54. Three quarters of the SO2 effect is SO2 per unit of CO2, that is, less sulphur emitted per unit of fossil fuel burned, which is the technique term; energy efficiency contributes the rest and the fuel mix nothing. The same holds for NOx (col 5 = cols 2+3+6) and in Panel B. The Kaya identity in col 7 shows that the (insignificant) CO2 effect is the sum of the energy-intensity and fuel-mix terms, as it must be with population and income held fixed.
A3: Dropping one GACI region at a time, the IV estimate for SO2 intensity is stable between −4 and −7.5 except when Europe is dropped: without Europe the instrument loses its first-stage power (F 3.1) and the estimate is +1.1 and insignificant. The market-access instrument therefore identifies the effect mainly off the European experience.
